# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 81 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 81 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_081_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 8, Chapter 4

**1** "And those who returned their rods two-thirds green and one-third withered — who are they?" I asked. He answered, "These are those who believed, but some of them denied the faith and are now repentant. **2** These shall live, for their repentance is genuine, and they shall not die. But those who denied and did not repent shall die." **3** "And those who returned their rods two-thirds withered and one-third green — who are these?" **4** He said, "These are those who believed but for the most part were double-minded; many of them were rich and involved in worldly affairs, and because of this they became unfaithful and did not serve God, placing worldly business before all else. Yet they never departed from God — a small portion of faith always remained in them." **5** "And those who returned rods with a small part green and almost all withered — these were double-minded and full of doubt, and their deeds were evil." **6** "Those who returned their rods entirely withered and moth-eaten," he said, "are those who denied the Lord and never returned to faith." **7** "And those who returned rods with very little green and the rest withered — these are they who heard the word of God and believed, but did not cleave to the Lord with their whole heart and did not practice righteousness. They had neither departed from God nor acted in righteousness." **8** "Lord," I asked, "who then is worthy to inhabit the tower?" "Only these," he said — "those who returned their rods completely green, who did not separate themselves from the living God, who were faithful and did not mingle with the world but remained unspotted, righteous in all their deeds."

---

### Translator's Note
Verse 8 is the definitive answer to the tower allegory: total commitment, unstained faith, and separation from worldly compromise. The "double-minded" (dipsuchos) of v. 4 is Hermas's signature diagnosis of the Roman Christian community. SOPHIA follows LOGOS throughout; PNEUMA's "ember of faith" in v. 4 is vivid but paraphrastic.
